halloran_1.title: Welcome to the shop
halloran_1.body:
Dear {name},

If you're reading this, the dock office found you, and the hangar is yours. I'm sorry about the state of it. Every drawer has a story and most of them end in "I'll finish that later."

A few things you should know. The kettle in the tea nook is temperamental, so tap it twice. The Kettle under the tarp in the back bay is a different kettle, and it's yours too. She was going to be my last project. She's slow, she's loud and I love her. Make her fly.

Pilots will come. They always do. Listen to what they ask for, then listen again for what they mean. The ship always tells you the rest.

I'm out past the comet line now, watching ice turn into fireworks. The tea here is terrible. I've never been happier.

With grease under every fingernail,
Halloran

P.S. Odessa Vell will stop by soon. Be kind to her Moth. That ship has carried more birthday presents than any freighter in the system.

P.P.S. Grommet comes with the shop. Pet when offered, never when not. If something goes missing, check the top of the drawers. If something turns up that you never owned, say thank you.

bulletin_1.title: Quietwater Dock Bulletin
bulletin_1.body:
DRUM GARDEN NEWS
The moon-plums are early this cycle. The gardeners ask that you stop eating them off the vine. You know who you are.

CLUB RACE TONIGHT
The weekly Quietwater Club Race runs three laps around the ring at last bell. Entry is free and so is the cocoa. Captain Marrow is defending her title for the forty-first week running and would like everyone to stop counting.

LOST AND FOUND
One (1) hat, knitted, with ear holes. Not for a human. Ask at the office.

GOSSIP CORNER
A certain maintenance unit was seen watching race replays through the observation glass until third shift. When asked, it said it was "studying joy." We have no further questions.

novel_1.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 1
novel_1.body:
Nobody had needed a lighthouse in Lumen Reach for ninety years, which is exactly why Wren Abara took the job.

The beacon still turned, out of habit more than purpose, sweeping its slow gold arm across a field of drifting ice. Ships had beacons of their own now, and maps, and minds that never got lost. Wren had a kettle, a cat named Corollary, and a logbook that the previous keeper had filled with nothing but weather.

"Calm," read one entry. "Calm again," read the next. Then, three hundred pages in, in handwriting gone wobbly with excitement: "A whale."

Wren read that entry four times. Then Wren put the kettle on, wrapped a blanket around both shoulders, and went up to the lamp room to wait.

Corollary, who did not believe in whales, went to sleep on the logbook.

(Chapter 2 arrives tomorrow.)

manual_hush.title: Hushdrive Owner's Pamphlet
manual_hush.body:
CONGRATULATIONS on your Hushdrive!

The Hushdrive's teardrop shell is lined with a woven dampening mesh that turns rattle into purr. Fitted to a small hauler it can cut cabin noise by half, and passengers report it "sounds like a cat thinking about a nap."

TINKERER'S NOTE (in Halloran's handwriting): Noise isn't just the drive. Cracked seams sing at speed. Weld them first, then swap the drive, and you'll hear the difference.

READING THIS PAMPHLET: you'll recognize Hushdrive fittings at a glance, and quiet-ride requests will make more sense to you.

odessa_letter_1.title: From the comet bloom
odessa_letter_1.body:
Dear {name},

We saw it! The whole sky went silver and pink, and the little ones pressed their noses to the glass and narrated every single sparkle. I heard every word. Every word! Do you know how long it's been since I heard a whole sentence from my grandson? He has opinions about comets. Many opinions.

The Moth hums now. My granddaughter says it sounds like a cat thinking about a nap. I don't know where she got that.

I'm thinking about something, and I'll tell you about it when I'm back through Quietwater. Keep the kettle warm.

Yours, with seed cake crumbs on the page,
Odessa

odessa_letter_1b.title: From the comet bloom
odessa_letter_1b.body:
Dear {name},

We saw it! The whole sky went silver and pink. The little ones pressed their noses to the glass and talked the whole way through. I caught about half of it, which is half more than last time.

The Moth still grumbles, bless her. Next time I'm through Quietwater, I think she and I need another visit.

Yours, with seed cake crumbs on the page,
Odessa

manual_pearl.title: The Pearl Lacquer Primer
manual_pearl.body:
PEARL LACQUER, A PRIMER

Pearl isn't a color. It's a promise that the color will change when you're not looking. Three thin coats over a warm base, each one buffed until you can see your own doubt in it.

TINKERER'S NOTE (in Halloran's handwriting): The rich ones always ask for pearl. Charge them for it. Then do it properly anyway, because the ship didn't do anything wrong.

READING THIS PRIMER: you can now lay down a pearl finish in the paint bay.

novel_2.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 2
novel_2.body:
Wren waited three nights for the whale.

On the first night Wren saw a comet, which was nice, and wrote it down. On the second night Wren saw a cargo hauler with one headlamp out, and radioed them about it, and they said thank you in the tone of people who would not be fixing it. On the third night Wren saw nothing at all and fell asleep in the lamp room with a cold cup of tea.

Corollary woke Wren at dawn by sitting on Wren's face.

The beacon had stopped turning.

It had never stopped turning, not in ninety years. Wren climbed up to check the gears and found them perfectly fine, and found something else instead: a long, pale, gentle shape drifting past the window, close enough to touch, its eye as big as the lamp, looking in.

Looking, Wren would swear for the rest of a long life, at the light.

(Chapter 3 arrives tomorrow.)

novel_3.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 3
novel_3.body:
The whale came back every night after that.

It never came closer than the first time, and it never stayed long. It drifted up out of the ice field, hung by the window while the beacon passed over it once, twice, three times, and then sank away again into the dark.

Wren started leaving the beacon on the slow setting. Then Wren started reading aloud, because it felt rude to just stare. Recipes, mostly, and the old keeper's weather log. Calm. Calm again.

Corollary, who still did not believe in whales, began sleeping on the windowsill.

(To be continued.)

bulletin_3.title: Quietwater Dock Bulletin
bulletin_3.body:
SHOP NEWS
The hangar at the end of Ring Four is open again under new management. Early reports describe the work as "careful," "cheerful," and "not too expensive," which is high praise on this dock.

CLUB RACE
Captain Marrow defended her title once more. A maintenance unit finished the race, came back to the start line, and asked if it could do it again. It was allowed.

REMINDER
The moon-plums are still not for picking.

bulletin_3b.title: Quietwater Dock Bulletin
bulletin_3b.body:
SHOP NEWS
The hangar at the end of Ring Four is open again under new management. Reports are mostly glowing, with one or two pilots muttering about "surprises." We're sure it's nothing.

CLUB RACE
Captain Marrow defended her title once more. A maintenance unit finished the race, came back to the start line, and asked if it could do it again. It was allowed.

REMINDER
The moon-plums are still not for picking.

brindle_letter_1.title: A report on corners
brindle_letter_1.body:
Dear {name},

I have taken the Bucket around the ring forty-one times since yesterday. I have attached a chart of my joy in corners. It goes up.

(There is no chart. Brindle has drawn a line going up, then a smiling face, then another line going up off the edge of the page.)

I have told everybody on the dock about your shop. Some of them did not ask. I told them anyway.

Your friend and rival,
Brindle

halloran_2.title: Ice and fireworks
halloran_2.body:
Dear {name},

Word travels slow out here, but it travels. Odessa sent me a message that was mostly exclamation marks. I gather you made her Moth purr.

A word of advice, since I can't help giving it. You'll get customers who are rude. Some of them will deserve a goose horn. Some of them will deserve worse. Remember that you have to live on that dock, and they'll remember you as long as you remember them.

That said. If Thaddeus Crake ever comes in, I left something in the second drawer from the left. It honks.

The comet bloom out here is starting. I've run out of words for it, so I'll stop.

Halloran

crake_letter_polite.title: Re: The Magnificence
crake_letter_polite.body:
{name},

The Magnificence performed acceptably at the yacht club regatta. Several people asked where she was serviced. I told them. You may expect a better class of customer.

Do not mistake this for gratitude.

T. Crake

crake_letter_prank.title: A STRONGLY WORDED LETTER
crake_letter_prank.body:
{name},

I have been unable to remove the item. I have consulted three engineers. One of them laughed so hard he had to sit down.

I want you to know that I am not amused, and that I will be returning, and that I am also, against my will, a little bit impressed.

This is not over.

T. Crake

P.S. The yacht club has started calling me "Honky." I hope you're happy.

crake_letter_sabotage.title: NOTICE OF GRIEVANCE
crake_letter_sabotage.body:
To the proprietor,

We write on behalf of our client, Mr. Thaddeus Crake, regarding an incident involving his yacht, the Magnificence, a regatta, and approximately forty cubic meters of packing foam (or smoke rings, or a hairpin; our client's account varies).

Our client demands the vessel be restored at your expense when next he docks.

Yours, with some reluctance, as Mr. Crake is not an easy client either,
Crake, Crake & Thistlewood

halloran_drawer.title: For later
halloran_drawer.body:
Dear {name},

If you've opened this drawer, it's later. Good. I hoped it would be.

I didn't leave because I was tired of the shop. I left because I'd stopped hearing the ships. You'll know what I mean soon if you don't already: the way a seam sings when it's about to go, the way an engine sighs when it's been treated kindly. I'd started fixing things by the manual instead of by ear, and that's no way to treat a ship, or a dock.

Out here past the comet line I'm learning to listen again. The comet bloom is coming, by the way. Odessa will want to see it. Everyone will. Go, if you can. Close the shop for a night.

Grommet knows where the good drawer is. Bribe accordingly.

With grease under every fingernail,
Halloran

race_calendar.title: Race calendar
race_calendar.body:
THE CLUB RACE
Every evening at last bell, around the Quietwater Ring. Open to all.

SLOW SUNDAY CUP (days 7, 14, 21...)
The Quietwater Ring, for gentle ships. Nothing rated over 175. Odessa Vell has entered, and says she intends to win, slowly.

RING SHADOW NIGHT RUN (days 3, 10, 17...)
A fast night course through Bramble's shadow, for Class B ships rated 245 or under.

DRUM GARDEN DASH (days 5, 12, 19...)
Three laps of the twistiest course on the dock, between the floating terrariums. Anything goes.

Your ship's race rating is on its readout at the workbench.

ilse_letter_1.title: A tenth
ilse_letter_1.body:
{name},

I've been thinking about that tenth of a second. Whether it was the ship or me. Whether it matters.

Halloran used to say that a pilot slows down the day they stop being curious. I'm still curious. About the Garden Dash, mostly. Twistiest course on the dock. I've won it eleven times and never once flown it the same way twice.

Don't tell Brindle I write letters. It'll want to read them aloud.

Ilse

crake_letter_mother.title: From Philippa Crake
crake_letter_mother.body:
Dear {name},

My son tells me you are the tinkerer who made our cabin quiet. He also tells me he was, and I quote, "perfectly civil." I do hope that's true. He has always been a dear boy underneath, but underneath is a long way down with Thaddeus.

I shall see the Close Pass from a seat that does not rattle, for the first time in twenty years. Thank you.

If he is ever rude to you again, write to me.

With regards,
Philippa Crake

halloran_3.title: I saw you
halloran_3.body:
Dear {name},

I watched the Close Pass from out past the comet line, and I swear I could see the dock's ships from here, a little ring of lights in the dark, all huddled together like they were sharing a blanket.

That's the shop, you know. Not the hangar, not the tools. The ring of lights.

I think I can hear the ships again. Out here it's quiet enough. I'll come back one day to visit, if you'll have me. Grommet will pretend not to know me. Grommet will be lying.

With grease under every fingernail,
Halloran

odessa_letter_roots.title: Unpacking
odessa_letter_roots.body:
Dear {name},

The flat above the drum gardens has a window that catches the morning misters, and in the afternoons the light comes through them in little rainbows. I've unpacked one box. I've been looking at the rainbows instead of the other boxes.

The grandkids are coming for a fortnight next month. You'll meet them. They have opinions about you already, mostly good, and one about your cat.

Seed cake on Thursdays. I'll bring it round.

Your neighbor,
Odessa

odessa_letter_roams.title: From somewhere over the third moon
odessa_letter_roams.body:
Dear {name},

Four of us in the Moth, and you were right, there's room. The littlest one sleeps in the cargo net. The oldest one has taken over navigation and we have been somewhat lost since Tuesday, which is the best I've felt in years.

We'll bring her back through Quietwater at the end of the summer. Have the kettle on.

Love from all four of us,
Odessa (and Pell, and Juno, and little Sorrel, who says hello to the cat)

brindle_joy_report.title: Joy report: final
brindle_joy_report.body:
Dear {name},

I have finished measuring joy.

Findings:
1. Corners: medium joy.
2. Twists: high joy.
3. Winning: high joy, but short.
4. Watching friends go zoom: highest joy. Lasts a long time.
5. Sitting still under a comet with everyone: off the scale. I had to invent a new scale. I have called it a {name}.

Conclusion: I will keep the Bucket, but I will mostly watch. The racing club has asked if I would like to talk over the speakers during races. I said yes before they finished asking.

Your friend,
Brindle

novel_4.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 4
novel_4.body:
In the spring the beacon's gears began to slip.

Not badly. A hitch in the sweep, a stutter in the gold arm as it crossed the ice, as if the light were catching its breath. Wren oiled the gears and tightened the bolts and read the old keeper's log for advice, but the log said only "Calm" and "Calm again" and, once, "Ask the tinkerer from Quietwater. They hear things."

The whale still came every night. But it came later now, and lingered at the window, and Wren began to wonder whether the whale came for the light at all, or whether it came because the light was the only thing out there that sang.

Corollary started sleeping in the lamp room. Corollary, it must be said, still did not believe in whales.

(To be continued.)

novel_5.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 5
novel_5.body:
On the longest night of the year, the beacon stopped.

Wren climbed the stairs two at a time and found the great lens still, the gold arm frozen halfway across the ice, and the gears humming a note Wren had never heard them hum before: low and lost, like a question.

Outside, the whale came up out of the ice field. It drifted to the window and waited, its eye as big as the lamp, and Wren understood all at once that it was not looking at the light. It was listening for it.

Wren sat down on the cold floor of the lamp room, put an arm around Corollary, and said aloud, to nobody, "I need someone who can hear what's wrong."

(The final chapter will be published when the author finds out how it ends.)

lumen_invite.title: A real lighthouse
lumen_invite.body:
Dear {name},

Forgive a stranger writing. I'm the author of the Lumen Reach serial, and I have a confession: it isn't entirely fiction.

There is a lighthouse at Lumen Reach, at the very edge of the rings, and I am its keeper. My name is Themba. Wren is a little braver than me, and Corollary is exactly as rude as my real cat. And the beacon really has stopped. I wrote chapter five on the cold floor of the lamp room.

The old keeper's log really does say "Ask the tinkerer from Quietwater. They hear things." That was Halloran, years ago. Halloran is gone past the comet line now, and the dock says you're the one who hears things these days.

Would you come? I can pay in tea, and in an ending.

With hope,
Themba Okonkwo-Hale
Keeper, Lumen Reach Light

novel_6.title: The Lighthouse Keeper of Lumen Reach, Chapter 6
novel_6.body:
The tinkerer came on the third night, in a small round ship that whistled when it braked.

They did not read the manual. They climbed to the lamp room, put a hand flat against the gear housing, and listened. Then they turned two dials a very small amount, and the gears hummed a different note, a sure one, and the gold arm swept out across the ice again as if it had never stopped.

The whale rose out of the ice field before the beam had crossed it twice. It sang, long and low, and the glass in the lamp room sang back.

Corollary watched the whale through the window for a very long time. Then Corollary sat down on the logbook, which is how a cat says: all right. I believe you now.

The End.

(Dedicated to the tinkerer of Quietwater, who hears things.)
